head:
Profiles · Teenagers · Ages 12 to 17

The teen who no longer moves: where to restart, and how to keep going

This article is for the teenager and their parents. It starts from a common case, a teenager who has stopped doing sport or never did any, and looks at what research allows us to say: what age changes, what motivates or blocks, what is safe, what needs watching. It ends with a twelve-week plan of three sessions. This plan is a proposal, not a programme that has been tested as it stands.

The question

A typical profile (illustrative, invented character). A 14-year-old. Two years ago they played for a club. Then secondary school got harder, friends stopped, and there was a coach or a changing room where they no longer felt at ease. Today they take the bus home, spend the evening on their phone and go to bed late. They say sport is boring or that they are bad at it. No known illness, no injury. Their parents worry, try to motivate them, and the conversation quickly turns into an argument.

This profile is not rare. An adult can impose a routine on themselves through discipline. A teenager is negotiating with a changing body, other people's gaze, sleep and school: they move if they feel like it, otherwise they do not.

The question

In a teenager aged 12 to 17, what really changes the way of getting back into sport, and what simple plan makes it possible to start again without getting injured or put off, and to keep going long enough for it to become normal?

What is at stake is concrete: the body (bone is mostly built now; article “Bone: a capital”), the mind (sleep, mood; article “Sport and mental health: what physical activity changes in the mind”), the habit, and the relationship between parents and teenager. The aim is not performance. It is to get a teenager moving again without damaging either their body or their desire to move.

The underlying plan for getting back in shape is shared by almost everyone: a little regular movement, strength work, slow progression, a measurement from time to time, sleep. What changes with the profile is the starting point, the dose, the risks specific to the age, the obstacles and the moment to ask for medical advice.

Step 1 of 6 · The starting point

The vast majority of teenagers do not move enough, everywhere, and girls even less

The WHO recommendation for ages 5 to 17 fits in two lines: on average at least 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous physical activity, mostly aerobic, and, at least three days a week, vigorous activity as well as activities that strengthen muscles and bones. It is classed as a “strong recommendation”, backed by evidence of moderate certainty.1

A WHO-supported team pooled 298 school surveys (1.6 million pupils aged 11 to 17, 146 countries). In 2016, 81% did not meet this recommendation: 77.6% of boys, 84.7% of girls. Since 2001, almost nothing has moved (80.1% and 85.1%). Girls were less active than boys in every country except four.2

In fifteen years, the share of teenagers who are not active enough has barely fallen

School surveys, ages 11-17, 146 countries; “insufficiently active” = less than 60 minutes a day of moderate to vigorous activity, self-reported. Source: Guthold et al., Lancet Child & Adolescent Health, 2020, read in a specialist press report.2

What this means

A teenager who does not move enough is in the vast majority, not an exception. These figures are reported by the pupils themselves: they give an order of magnitude.

What remains is to see what, in adolescence itself, makes getting moving again different.

Step 2 of 6 · What age changes

The body changes fast, and not at the same time for everyone

In a Canadian study that follows children to measure their bone, peak growth in height occurs on average around age 11.8 in girls and 13.5 in boys. The biggest gains in bone mass occur in the five years around this peak; they are much smaller afterwards. The bone gained during childhood and adolescence is about double what is lost at the end of adult life.3

To go further: article “Bone: a capital built before age 30”. Why loading and impact matter during growth.

Two teenagers of the same age can differ by four to five years in biological maturity (2014 consensus on youth resistance training).4 A teenager who has grown 15 cm this year and another who has not started are not training in the same situation: they should not compare themselves.

In a meta-analysis of 42 studies (1,728 young people under 18), strength training improved strength more than in control groups, with a larger effect during or after puberty (1.91) than before (0.81). Pubertal stage explained the effect better than age in years.5

Strength responds more strongly to training once puberty is under way

Meta-analysis by Behringer et al., Pediatrics, 2010: 42 controlled studies, 1,728 young people, average study quality 4.9 out of 10 (PEDro scale), non-randomised studies included. Read in the PEDro commentary. Effect size cannot be converted into a percentage of strength.5

What this means

Before puberty, strength improves mainly through coordination; afterwards muscle joins in too, especially in boys.4 The studies are of average quality: treat this as an order of magnitude.

Girls and boys: a real gap, a “drop-off” to be qualified

You hear that girls “drop off” in adolescence. The gap in level is real (step 1). The timing of the drop-off is less so: in a British cohort of 545 children measured by accelerometer at ages 7, 9, 12 and 15, all trajectories declined from age 7, with no evidence that the decline was steeper in adolescence or in girls. But about 19% of boys kept a high, stable level of vigorous activity, and no comparable group appeared among girls.6

According to a survey by Canadian Women and Sport (more than 10,000 people), about one girl in three who has played sport drops out towards the end of adolescence, compared with about one boy in ten among 16-18 year olds.7 Reasons given: lack of confidence, negative body image, feeling bad at it or not welcome. A New Zealand review adds a changing body, revealing kit, an overly judgemental atmosphere, comments about appearance.8 These are surveys, not trials: they tell us what girls report, not what would make them stay.

For parents

For a girl: never comment on her body in connection with sport, let her choose an activity where she is comfortable (kit, group, atmosphere), and accept that recreational practice may suit her better than competition. I have not read any data on body image in boys: do not conclude anything from that.

Step 3 of 6 · Motivation and autonomy

People keep going when the desire comes from within, not from pressure

Self-determination theory distinguishes autonomous motivation (I do it because I like it or because it matters to me) from controlled motivation (to avoid punishment or shame, or because I am told to). In adults, Teixeira’s review (66 studies) finds autonomous motivation linked to more activity, with enjoyment itself better predicting long-term practice. External pressure is negatively linked to activity in 16 independent samples (43%).9 This review excludes children and teenagers.

For young people, Owen’s meta-analysis (46 studies, nearly 16,000 children and teenagers) finds a moderate association between autonomous motivation and activity (0.27 to 0.38), weak and negative for controlled motivation (-0.17 to -0.03) and for amotivation (-0.21 to -0.11), with strong heterogeneity.10

Desire that comes from within goes with more activity, pressure goes with a little less

How to read: each bar runs from the lowest to the highest published estimate depending on how it was measured. Source: Owen et al., Preventive Medicine, 2014 (abstract), 46 studies, 15,984 young people.10

What this means

These are associations: a teenager who moves may have more desire because they move. But the direction is consistent: the more the desire comes from them, the more they move.

In adults, a sense of competence is linked to activity in 56% of samples, with autonomy giving more mixed results.9 Choosing an activity where the teenager feels they are progressing therefore matters at least as much as letting them choose.

For parents

These studies do not say “let them do whatever they want”. They say that the pressure of “you must” tends to go with less activity. Offer a menu of three to five activities that suit you, let them choose, accept that they change, and do not link sport to grades or punishments.

Step 4 of 6 · Screens, sleep, mind

Sleep is the first casualty of screens, and it conditions everything else

A review of 67 studies on screen time and young people’s sleep finds that 90% point the same way: shorter sleep, later falling asleep; the authors write that the mechanisms and magnitude remain to be understood.11 The American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours per 24 hours for 13-18 year olds; regularly sleeping less is associated with attention problems, more injuries and an increased risk of depression and suicidal thoughts.12 Before adding sessions, it is better to protect bedtime. My proposal, with no intervention study read: phone out of the bedroom at night, session at the latest in the late afternoon.

Before adding sessions, it is better to protect bedtime. What I propose, without having read it in an intervention study: keep the phone out of the bedroom at night, and hold the evening session in the late afternoon at the latest.

Mental health: article “Sport and mental health: what physical activity changes in the mind”. What sport changes in mood, what is solid or not, and what to do in case of distress (in France, 3114 is the national suicide prevention number). If your teenager has been sad, irritable or withdrawn for weeks, this is a matter for a doctor or a psychologist, not for a training plan.
Step 5 of 6 · Strength, safety, growth

Supervised strength training is safe at this age, the fear for growth is unfounded

The 2014 international consensus (Lloyd) and the 2009 NSCA statement (Faigenbaum) say the same thing: a well-designed, supervised programme is relatively safe, fears for growth plates are not supported, and no evidence shows a negative effect on height. The old cases of injury were linked to poor technique, maximal loads or lack of supervision.4,13

Benchmarks from these texts: two to three sessions a week on non-consecutive days, a dynamic warm-up of 5 to 10 minutes, technique before load. A beginner starts with one or two sets at no more than 60% of maximum, then moves to two to four sets of 6 to 12 repetitions at no more than 80%, with steps of 5 to 10%. Strength gains of 30 to 40% are typical in untrained young people after 8 to 20 weeks.4,13 As for risk, strength training accounted for 0.7% of the 1,576 injuries in a school study cited by the NSCA; the lower back is the most affected area; most acute injuries are accidental (77%) and avoidable through supervision and reasonable progression.4,13

What this means

What is dangerous: maximal load, poor technique, the absence of a qualified adult and equipment misused at home. Without a qualified adult, stay with body weight and keep the session short.

Step 6 of 6 · What can go wrong

Diets, appearance culture, overtraining and growing pains

Diets and appearance

There will be no diet advice here. In a study of 2,516 teenagers followed for five years (Project EAT-II), dieting at baseline predicted more binge eating in both sexes, fewer breakfasts in girls and less activity in boys, and these behaviours went with a gain in body mass index.14 It is an association, but a consistent one: dieting is not a good starting point at this age.

The International Olympic Committee consensus describes relative energy deficiency in sport (RED-S): when the energy taken in does not cover the energy spent, periods, bone, immunity and the cardiovascular system are affected (absent periods, low bone density).15 While bone is being built, this is a real risk. The New Zealand review advises seeking advice if the first period has not occurred by age 15.8

For parents

These are signals, not a diagnosis: rapid weight loss, avoided or counted meals, guilt if a session is skipped, training in addition to the planned sessions, periods that disappear, refusing to eat in front of others. They warrant medical advice, not a debate at the table. Avoid comments about physical appearance, including positive ones.

Too much, too fast, too specialised

In a case-control study of 1,190 athletes aged 7 to 18, early specialisation in a single sport was an independent risk of serious overuse injury; growth rate was not linked to the risk (4.8 cm a year in both groups).16 This is not our profile, but it is why the plan stays varied and moderate.

Growing pains in the knee and heel

Two pains come up repeatedly. Osgood-Schlatter disease is a traction apophysitis below the kneecap, attributed to overloading of the quadriceps during growth (knee pain on exertion, swelling); it resolves with bone maturity.17 Sever’s disease is the same at the heel, mostly between ages 9 and 12, usually without lasting effects, improving within 6 to 12 months with activity adapted to the pain.18 This is not a reason to stop all sport, but they should be discussed with a doctor, especially if the pain is strong, atypical or persists.

What makes people keep going: the main obstacle is adherence

Knowing what to do is not the hard part: it is doing it again and again. Three tools have evidence, with one caveat: none was read here in teenagers.

A habit takes two months on average, and varies widely between people

Lally et al., 2010: 82 adult students over 84 days, one chosen behaviour repeated every day; self-reported automaticity. The 254 is an estimate by extrapolation. Read via a British Psychological Society summary.19

What this means

The twelve-week plan lasts 84 days, the length of this study. This is not a promise that it will be automatic at the end: the length varies a great deal from one person to another. Missing one day has little effect, missing often does. The study is on adult students, not teenagers.

First tool: the “if-then” plan. A meta-analysis of 94 tests (Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006, read via a summary site) finds that a plan of the type “when this situation arises, I do this action” helps in reaching a goal (effect of about 0.65).20 Example: “If it’s Tuesday 17:30 and I get home, I put my bag down and put my shoes on.” Second tool: self-monitoring. In a meta-regression of 122 evaluations, combining self-monitoring with another control technique gives an effect of 0.42 versus 0.26 otherwise.21 In practice: a calendar, one cross per session. Third tool: autonomy, seen above.

For parents

Your role is not to remind: it is to make the plan easy (bag ready, free slot, journey sorted). You can do one session a week with them if that is their choice. A missed week: carry on without comment.

The action plan: twelve weeks, three sessions

Here is the trajectory I propose. Proposal It combines what the texts read say about dose (WHO, consensus on youth strength training) with session choices that I have not seen tested as they stand. It does not replace medical advice or a qualified coach. Three sessions are not enough on their own to reach the WHO’s 60 minutes a day: they are the core, the rest comes from walking, walking or cycling to places and free play. But they do cover the guidance of three days a week of vigorous activity and of muscle and bone strengthening.1

Three sessions a week, which lengthen a little and are shared between play, strength and endurance

In each bar, from bottom to top: play (light grey), strength (grey), endurance (accent colour). Proposed values, not taken from a study. The 420 minutes a week of the WHO recommendation are not reached by these sessions alone.

Before starting

Week 0: the check, the measurement, the calendar

Health. Fill in the PAR-Q+ questionnaire, valid for all ages: seven questions. If all the answers are “no”, you can resume gradually. If one is “yes”, there are follow-up questions and, depending on the case, a discussion with a qualified professional or the doctor; about 1% of people are referred for a medical evaluation.22 Also talk to the doctor if your teenager has a known illness, a treatment, faintness on exertion, a heart murmur, poorly controlled asthma, or a history of eating disorder.

Measurement. Do the THW endurance, strength and mobility/balance tests from the page, once, cold. The norm tables on the page are not designed for 12-17 year olds: use them to compare yourself with yourself, not with others. Retest in weeks 6 and 12.

System. Three fixed slots in the week, written down. An if-then plan for each, a calendar with one cross per session. One session in three is chosen by the teenager.

Weeks 1 to 4

Return to enjoyment and learn the movements

SessionContentDose
A. PlayA game chosen by the teenager: team sport, badminton, basketball, ultimate, tag, dance, climbing, active walk. A few short jumps and landings, but free intensity.50 min
B. Technical strengthDynamic warm-up 5 to 10 minutes. Five or six movements: squat to a bench, incline push-up, band row, hip hinge (glute bridge), plank, bag carry. Body weight or light load.35 min, 1 to 2 sets of 10 to 15 repetitions, 1 minute rest
C. Easy enduranceBrisk walking, cycling, swimming, jog-walk, with a friend. A pace at which you can talk. Either 20 to 30 continuous minutes, or 5 times 3 minutes active and 2 minutes easy.35 min

What session B looks like, step by step. Proposal

  1. Warm-up, 8 minutesBrisk walking, shoulder circles, body-weight squats, knee raises. Dynamic, no static stretching before the effort.13
  2. Lower bodySquat to a bench, then glute bridge: one or two sets of 10 to 15, slowly, knees in line with the feet.
  3. Upper bodyPush-up with hands on a piece of furniture or the wall, then band row: one or two sets of 10 to 15.
  4. Plank and carry, 5 minutesPlank for 15 to 30 seconds, walking with a lightly loaded bag.
  5. Cool-downSlow walking, a few stretches. If a repetition becomes laboured, technique takes priority: stop before it.

Progress: nothing to increase during these four weeks, except regularity. Stay: if fewer than two sessions in three took place for more than a week, repeat the week. Step back: any pain that lasts more than 24 hours or increases from one session to the next: reduce, then seek advice if it persists.

Weeks 5 to 8

Build

SessionContentDose
A. Play and speedSame choice, with short running and change-of-direction games. Full recovery between efforts.45 min
B. StrengthSame movements, plus a lunge or a step-up onto a bench. If technique is clean, a light dumbbell load for the squat or the hinge.45 min, 2 to 3 sets of 8 to 12 repetitions
C. Varied enduranceSpeed play: 6 times (1 minute faster, 2 minutes easy), or a bike ride with a goal (a place, a friend).45 min

Progress: when the last high set is held with clean technique in two sessions in a row, increase the load by 5 to 10%, as the texts on young people recommend.13 Retest in week 6: endurance, strength, mobility/balance. Compare yourself with week 0, nothing else.

Weeks 9 to 12

Consolidate

SessionContentDose
A. Play and challengeA regular appointment: signing up for a club or group activity, or a small tournament among friends.45 min
B. StrengthSame movements, more load. Stay within the benchmarks of the texts: 2 to 4 sets of 6 to 12 repetitions, low to moderate load. No maximal load test.50 min
C. Endurance25 to 35 continuous minutes at conversation pace, or 4 times (4 minutes sustained, 3 minutes easy).55 min

Retest in week 12: the three tests. Move on to maintenance if at least nine sessions out of twelve took place, if technique is clean and if the teenager wants to continue. Otherwise, stay one more phase: this is not a failure, it is the pace.

All phases

Decision rules and adaptations

SituationDecision Proposal
At least 2 sessions out of 3 for 3 weeks out of 4, clean technique, no painMove on to the next phase.
A week with 0 or 1 sessionRepeat the week, without making up the missed sessions.
Localised pain in the knee, heel or back that lasts more than 24 hoursReduce jumping and load for a week. If it persists, increases or wakes them at night: medical advice.
Several short nights in a rowReplace the strength session with walking and light play; put sleep first again.
A retest worse than the previous oneLook first at sleep and regularity before changing the plan; a test is one marker among others.

In the middle of a growth spurt. If the knee or heel pulls after jumping, replace part of the impact play with cycling or swimming and talk to a doctor about it (see above). Girl. Note periods on the tracking calendar, adapt intensity on difficult days, and impose nothing about kit or group. Boy. The trap is loading too much: the ceiling remains that of the texts, never the maximal load. Teenager who has already played sport. Start with phase 1 all the same: the movements come back quickly, tendons and desire take time.

After week 12

Maintain, vary, do not stop everything

Keep three sessions, or two sessions plus free movement, depending on the season, school, exams. Redo the tests every three months. Change one of the play activities each term. If a busy period interrupts everything, restart from phase 1 without guilt: it is the same principle as for all profiles, repeating again and again.

Common mistakes, warning signs, when to consult

Common mistakes. Aiming for performance from the start; linking sport to grades or punishment; comparing the teenager with a classmate; lifting heavy because a friend does; skipping the warm-up; talking about weight or appearance.

Medical advice before or during the plan if: a “yes” answer on the PAR-Q+; chest pain, faintness, palpitations or breathlessness out of proportion to the effort; strong knee or heel pain, with limping, waking at night, lasting or increasing; swelling, redness or warmth of a joint; absent periods at 15, or periods that disappear; rapid weight loss, food restriction, compulsive exercise; fatigue that does not go away. This list is general help, not a diagnosis: the PAR-Q+ questionnaire and the doctor remain the reference. For mood, see the article “Sport and mental health: what physical activity changes in the mind”.

Answer to the question

Four things are solid. The vast majority of teenagers do not move enough, girls most of all: your case is ordinary. Supervised strength training is safe and useful at this age, with light loads and technique first, and it does not slow growth. Bone is mostly built during these years, which gives value to strength and impact. And 8 to 10 hours of sleep is the foundation.

What is probable but based on associations: desire that comes from within goes with more activity in young people, pressure with a little less. What is a proposal: the three sessions, the durations, the order of the phases, the choice of games and movements. What is uncertain: the timing of girls’ “drop-off”, the effect of screens beyond sleep, and the best way to keep going at 14, because the adherence tools come from adult populations. The plan is simple if the teenager is ready to start. If they are not, the problem is not the plan, it is the desire, and parents and teenager have to work on it together.

Limitations
  • Most studies on motivation and habits are associations or concern adults; teenagers’ activity figures are self-reported.
  • The plan has not been tested as it stands; it applies the benchmarks of the consensus texts on youth strength training and of the WHO.
  • The norm tables of the THW tests for 12-17 year olds were not provided; the article proposes comparing yourself with yourself.

Frequently asked questions

Does my teenager have to do 60 minutes a day from the start?

No. The target is an average over the week, and you get there gradually. The three sessions are the core, the rest comes from walking or cycling to places and free play.1

Will strength training slow their growth?

The two consensus statements read say no: no evidence of a negative effect on growth, and no cartilage damage in prospective studies.4,13 The condition is supervision and technique.

What if they refuse everything?

Reduce the goal: a single activity chosen by them, ten minutes, once a week, with a calendar. If the refusal comes with lasting sadness, isolation or irritability, talk to a doctor (article “Sport and mental health: what physical activity changes in the mind”).
